cards.title: Strategic vs Tactical Design
cards.teaser: DDD splits into two distinct layers of practice: strategic design answers 'what are we building and where does it live in the business?'; tactical design answers 'how do we model it in code?' Neither layer works well without the other.

runs.text: Eric Evans organised
Domain-Driven Design

(2003) around a fundamental division. Before writing a single aggregate or repository, a team must answer coarser questions: Which part of the problem space is genuinely novel? Where should the model live? Who owns it? Those questions belong to
strategic design
Vaughn Vernon, in
Implementing Domain-Driven Design

(2013), calls strategic design the most important part of DDD — and the most frequently skipped. Teams jump to entities, value objects, and repositories, then wonder why the model feels wrong after six months. The model feels wrong because the boundary was drawn wrong, and boundary decisions are strategic.

items.text: Strategic design
— subdomains, bounded contexts, context maps, ubiquitous language, and team topology. These decisions are made once and changed rarely; getting them wrong is expensive.
Tactical design

— aggregates, entities, value objects, domain events, repositories, and domain services. These patterns live inside a bounded context and can be refactored within the boundary without affecting others.

runs.text: A useful analogy: strategic design is urban planning — decide where the residential zones, industrial zones, and parks go. Tactical design is architecture — decide how to lay out the rooms inside a building. You can renovate the rooms, but you cannot easily move the building.

Evans's chapter on Strategic Design (Part IV of DDD) was written last and nearly cut from the book. He later said it was the most important part. Vernon's distillation in IDDD starts with strategic design deliberately — a course correction the community took years to absorb.

Strategic design answers 'what are we building, where does it live, and who owns it?' Tactical design answers 'how do we model it in code?' You need both, but getting the strategic layer right first saves you from building the right things in the wrong places.

cards.title: Domain vs Subdomain
cards.teaser: The domain is the entire business universe the software operates in. A subdomain is an analyzable slice of that universe — the unit of investment decision. Every real domain is too large to model as one thing; subdomains are how you carve it apart.

runs.text: Evans uses the word
domain

to mean the entire sphere of knowledge and activity the organisation operates in. An insurance company's domain includes underwriting, claims, policy administration, actuarial science, reinsurance, and regulatory compliance. That is far too large to model uniformly.
A
subdomain

is a coherent part of the domain that can be reasoned about independently. Underwriting is a subdomain. Claims processing is another. They have different experts, different rules, different vocabularies, and different rates of change. Decomposing the domain into subdomains is a discovery activity — it emerges from talking to domain experts, not from reading the org chart.
Subdomains are part of the
problem space
— they exist regardless of whether you build software. Bounded contexts are part of the
solution space

— they are decisions you make about how software models and owns the subdomains. The distinction matters: two bounded contexts can implement one subdomain (legacy + new), and one bounded context can cover multiple related subdomains.

The domain/subdomain split is not a software architecture decision — it is a business analysis decision. If your subdomains look like microservices, you have confused the problem space with the solution space. Subdomains are found; bounded contexts are designed.

The domain is everything the business does. A subdomain is one coherent slice of that — small enough to reason about, large enough to be meaningful. You discover subdomains by talking to experts; you design bounded contexts to model them in software.

cards.title: Core Subdomain
cards.teaser: The core subdomain is what makes your business uniquely valuable — the part competitors cannot easily replicate. It deserves your best engineers, deepest investment, and most sophisticated models. Outsourcing or simplifying the core is a strategic mistake.

runs.text: Vernon's distillation framework (IDDD, Chapter 2) identifies the
core subdomain

as the source of competitive advantage. For a ride-sharing company, dynamic pricing and driver-matching algorithms are core. For a bank, the credit risk model is core. These capabilities are why customers choose you over alternatives.
Core subdomain characteristics:

items.text: Competitors cannot easily replicate it.
It is proprietary knowledge, unique data, or hard-won expertise.
It changes frequently as the business learns.
A static subdomain is a sign it has become generic.
Domain experts actively care about its correctness.
If nobody can explain what makes it special, it probably is not core.
It should never be outsourced or bought off-the-shelf.
Buying a core subdomain means buying a competitor's version of your differentiation.

runs.text: The correct investment posture for the core: apply DDD's full tactical toolbox, assign senior engineers, accept higher complexity in exchange for precision, and iterate the model continuously with domain experts. The core subdomain is where the effort pays off.

Many teams treat everything as core and apply sophisticated DDD patterns everywhere. This is wasteful. A disciplined core/supporting/generic split lets you invest deeply where it matters and keep costs low everywhere else.

The core subdomain is the thing your business does that competitors cannot easily copy. It is the reason you exist. Build it yourself, model it carefully, and never outsource it — that would be outsourcing your competitive advantage.

cards.title: Supporting Subdomain
cards.teaser: A supporting subdomain is necessary for the business to operate, but it does not differentiate you from competitors. The build-or-buy decision is live: you might build it to maintain control, but a vendor solution is on the table.

runs.text: The
supporting subdomain

enables the core but cannot exist independently as the source of competitive advantage. A delivery company's route optimization is core; its driver onboarding workflow is supporting. The onboarding process must exist and work correctly, but no customer chooses the company because of onboarding excellence.
Distinguishing features of a supporting subdomain:

items.text: Custom enough that off-the-shelf solutions do not fit exactly,
but not unique enough to be a source of competitive advantage.
Requires domain knowledge to build correctly,
but the domain is moderately stable — not the frontier of your business.
Acceptable to staff with mid-level engineers.
Reserve your most senior people for the core.

runs.text: The build decision is defensible for supporting subdomains when vendor lock-in risk is high, integration cost is prohibitive, or the subdomain will eventually migrate toward core. But the bar should be explicit: this is not core, so the investment ceiling is lower and the tolerance for technical sophistication is also lower.

A supporting subdomain is necessary but not differentiating. You cannot buy it off-the-shelf because it is too specific to your business, but it also is not what makes you special. Build it, but do not over-engineer it.

cards.title: Generic Subdomain
cards.teaser: A generic subdomain is a solved problem — authentication, accounting, email delivery, CMS. The answer is almost always 'buy', and the interesting design question shifts from 'how do we build this?' to 'how do we integrate it cleanly without letting it leak into our core model?'

runs.text: The
generic subdomain

exists in virtually every business domain and has been solved well by the market. Authentication (Auth0, Okta), accounting (QuickBooks, Xero), full-text search (Elasticsearch, Algolia), email delivery (SendGrid), and CMS (Contentful, WordPress) are all generic subdomains. Building them from scratch consumes engineering capacity that should go toward the core.

The canonical answer for a generic subdomain is: buy a best-of-breed solution and integrate it behind an abstraction. The abstraction matters. If the vendor's model bleeds directly into your domain model — if you have Stripe
Customer
objects mixed with your own
Customer
entities — you have a translation problem that will cause pain when you switch vendors.

items.text: Always buy.
The market has invested far more in Auth0 than you will.
Isolate behind an abstraction.
Your domain model should speak your language; the generic subdomain integration is a peripheral adapter.
Apply an Anti-Corruption Layer if necessary.
See Chapter 4 — translating between the vendor's model and yours keeps your core clean.

runs.text: A common trap: teams build a custom payment processing system because the integrations 'looked complex.' Payments are generic. The complexity of integrating Stripe is far lower than the complexity of maintaining PCI DSS compliance on homegrown payment infrastructure.

Generic subdomains are solved problems. Buy them, hide them behind an abstraction, and move on. Every hour spent building your own authentication is an hour not spent on the thing that makes you different.

cards.title: Bounded Context
cards.teaser: A bounded context is the explicit linguistic and model boundary within which a domain model is defined and consistent. It is arguably the single most important concept in DDD — the one that makes everything else coherent.

runs.text: Evans introduced the
bounded context
in Part IV of DDD as the answer to a specific problem: a large system accumulates multiple teams, each developing their own model, and the models collide. The word
Customer
means different things to Sales, Billing, and Support. When these models merge into one codebase, every change to the shared
Customer
class ripples across the system in unpredictable ways.
A bounded context draws a hard line: inside this boundary, words have precise definitions and the model is internally consistent.
Customer
in the Billing context has billing address, payment methods, and invoice history.
Customer
in the Support context has tickets, sentiment score, and communication history. They share an identifier but are different objects with different purposes.
What a bounded context contains:

items.text: A domain model
— aggregates, entities, value objects, domain services, and domain events that are internally consistent.
A ubiquitous language
— the shared vocabulary used by both the team and the code inside the boundary.
A defined interface
— how other contexts interact with this one (APIs, events, or shared kernel).
An owning team
— a bounded context without a team owning it decays.

runs.text: Evans says in the DDD Reference (2015): 'A model only exists in the context of its application. Context is the setting that determines the meaning of any statement.' The bounded context is the formalisation of that insight — it makes the setting explicit and enforced.

A bounded context is a hard boundary around a model. Inside that boundary, every word has a precise, agreed meaning. Outside it, the same word might mean something different. The boundary is what lets large teams build large systems without a shared-model collision.

cards.title: Ubiquitous Language
cards.teaser: Ubiquitous language is the shared vocabulary that domain experts and developers use inside a bounded context — precise enough to become class names, method names, and event names, and spoken aloud in every meeting and document within the context.

runs.text: Evans's most actionable insight in the tactical layer is also strategic: when the language the team speaks is the language the code speaks, a whole category of translation error disappears.
Ubiquitous language
is not a glossary document; it is the living vocabulary enforced by both conversation and code.
What ubiquitous language looks like in practice:

items.text: Domain experts and developers use the same terms in meetings.
If the expert says 'policy' and the code says 'contract', there is translation friction that will eventually cause a bug.
Class names, method names, and event names match domain vocabulary.
Policy.lapse()
says the same thing the actuary says.
The language evolves.
When the domain expert changes terminology, the code changes. Frozen language means the model is drifting from reality.
Ambiguous words are resolved, not avoided.
If 'order' means something different in fulfillment versus billing, the language forces a decision: are these different concepts, or one concept with two projections?

runs.text: Ubiquitous language is bounded: it applies within one bounded context. The word 'account' means something precise in Banking and something different in Identity. The bounded context is the scope of the language's validity.

A ubiquitous language that exists in a glossary but not in the code is not ubiquitous. The code is the ground truth. If the code uses different words than the domain experts, the language is not established — it is aspirational.

Ubiquitous language means engineers and domain experts use exactly the same words — not a translation layer, not synonyms. When the business says 'policy lapse', the code has a method called 'lapse' on a class called 'Policy'. The language is the contract between the domain and the code.

cards.title: The Bounded Context = Subdomain Rule (or Not)
cards.teaser: Ideally, one bounded context implements one subdomain. In practice they diverge — legacy systems, team structures, and acquisition history all bend the line. Understanding when they match and when they do not is essential for reading existing systems honestly.

runs.text: The
ideal

is a one-to-one mapping: each subdomain has exactly one bounded context responsible for it, owned by exactly one team, with its own model and language. This is clean, legible, and gives the best alignment between problem space and solution space.
Reality is messier. Several divergence patterns are common:

items.text: One bounded context spans multiple subdomains.
This often happens in monoliths where a single codebase grew to cover several business areas. The model is under strain — multiple ubiquitous languages compete inside the same boundary.
Multiple bounded contexts implement one subdomain.
Classic during migrations: a legacy system and a new system both model 'customer', and both are in production. The context map must make explicit which is authoritative.
A subdomain has no bounded context.
The capability exists as ad hoc code distributed across several services. This is technical debt in the problem-to-solution mapping.

runs.text: Vernon's guidance: recognise the current state on a context map, then use the map to drive refactoring toward the ideal over time. Do not pretend the one-to-one ideal exists when it does not — the pretense makes the map useless.

Acquired companies are a rich source of context/subdomain divergence. Two product lines built independently arrive at an integration project with two different models of the same subdomain. The context map is the starting point for the integration conversation.

One subdomain, one bounded context is the goal. Reality often has one context covering too many subdomains, or two contexts covering the same subdomain because of history. Map reality honestly, then work toward the ideal incrementally.

cards.title: Context Map
cards.teaser: The context map is the system-level diagram showing every bounded context and how they relate to each other. Evans dedicated a chapter to it; teams that skip it navigate a large distributed system by folklore rather than by design.

runs.text: Evans introduced the context map in Chapter 14 of DDD as the answer to a specific problem: once you have multiple bounded contexts, you need an honest picture of how they integrate. The context map is not an aspirational architecture diagram — it documents
reality as it is
, including legacy systems, vendor integrations, and awkward seams.
A minimal context map shows:

items.text: Every bounded context
as a named box (include third-party systems and legacy as boxes).
Every integration

as a labeled line (the relationship pattern: shared kernel, customer/supplier, conformist, anti-corruption layer, open host service, published language, partnership, or separate ways — see Chapter 4).
Upstream/downstream direction
on each line — who provides the model and who consumes it.

runs.text: An ASCII sketch of a four-context map for an e-commerce system:

items.text: Context map (ASCII):

[Order Management] --ACL--> [Inventory]
         |                         |
    OHS/PL                    Conformist
         |                         |
         v                         v
  [Payment (Stripe)]      [Shipping (external)]

  Key:
  ACL  = Anti-Corruption Layer (Order translates Inventory's model)
  OHS  = Open Host Service (Payment publishes a stable API)
  PL   = Published Language (canonical payment event schema)
  Conformist = Shipping adapter adopts Inventory's address model as-is

runs.text: The relationship labels carry real design information. A Conformist relationship means the downstream context accepts the upstream's model without translation — a deliberate decision with known maintenance consequences. An ACL means the downstream context protects itself from the upstream's model.

Evans (DDD Chapter 14): 'Without an overall view of the relationships between contexts, we can easily get lost. A context map shows the real landscape, enabling informed decisions about where to put effort and what integration patterns to use.'

A context map is the honest diagram of every bounded context in the system and how they talk to each other. It includes messy reality — legacy systems, vendor boxes, conformist hacks. The map is how a team navigates a complex system without relying on folklore.

cards.title: Conway's Law and Bounded Contexts
cards.teaser: Conway's Law states that systems mirror the communication structure of the organisations that build them. Applied to DDD: team boundaries naturally become context boundaries. You can fight this, or design with it — designing with it is almost always more effective.

runs.text: Melvin Conway observed in 1967 that 'organisations which design systems are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organisations.' The inverse — the Inverse Conway Manoeuvre, popularised by the Team Topologies authors Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais — says: if you want a specific architecture, restructure the teams to mirror it first.
DDD's bounded contexts and Conway's Law are deeply linked:

items.text: A bounded context without a clear team owner decays.
Multiple teams writing to the same bounded context blur the language and model — they each introduce their own terms.
A team split across two bounded contexts creates friction.
The team must context-switch models, and the seam between the contexts often becomes underdefined because it is a seam within the team's own cognition.
Org restructuring breaks context ownership.
When a team is reorganised, the bounded contexts it owned become contested or orphaned — a leading indicator of model degradation.

runs.text: The practical implication: when drawing bounded contexts, look at the team topology. If the context map and the org chart are radically misaligned, you have either the wrong context map or the wrong org chart. Resolving the misalignment is a strategic decision.

Vernon explicitly links team ownership to bounded contexts in IDDD: 'One team owns one bounded context. When multiple teams own a context, the context needs a shared kernel or political coordination to stay coherent.' Team Topologies (Skelton and Pais, 2019) operationalises this with Stream-Aligned Teams as the pattern for context ownership.

Conway's Law says teams build systems that look like themselves. In DDD terms, a bounded context needs one owning team. If two teams write to the same context, the model fragments. Design your team topology and your context boundaries together — they are the same decision viewed from two angles.

cards.title: Translation Between Contexts
cards.teaser: When two bounded contexts communicate, their different models and languages must be translated at the boundary. This translation is not incidental complexity — it is the cost of having clear, clean models inside each context. Chapter 4 will cover the full integration pattern catalogue.

runs.text: Different bounded contexts will have different — sometimes contradictory — representations of the same real-world concept. An
Order

in the Fulfilment context has warehouse location, picking status, and packer ID. The same order in the Billing context has line items, tax breakdown, and payment status. Both are 'Order', but they are different projections of the same underlying event.
Translation approaches previewed here (detailed in Chapter 4):

items.text: Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)

— the downstream context wraps the upstream's model with a translation layer that speaks the downstream's language. The upstream model never leaks into the downstream domain. This is the safest pattern for integrating with legacy or vendor systems.
Open Host Service + Published Language
— the upstream context provides a stable, versioned API and a canonical schema. Downstream contexts can integrate without building custom translations. Used when one upstream serves many downstreams.
Conformist
— the downstream context adopts the upstream's model unchanged. Simple to implement; the downstream takes on the cognitive and maintenance burden of the upstream's model.
Shared Kernel
— two contexts share a small, explicitly agreed subset of the domain model. Changes to the shared kernel require coordination between both teams. High integration but high governance cost.

runs.text: The key principle: translation happens
at the boundary

, never inside a model. If Billing domain objects contain Fulfilment-specific fields 'just for convenience', the boundary has been violated. Model pollution is the consequence of skipping translation.

When two bounded contexts talk to each other, their different vocabularies have to be translated at the boundary. That translation is explicit and intentional — it is what keeps each context's model clean. The alternative is letting models bleed together, which defeats the purpose of having bounded contexts at all.

cards.title: Bounded Context Size
cards.teaser: A bounded context can be too big or too small. Too big: multiple competing models strain the language and create change coupling. Too small: excessive inter-context integration dominates development time and obscures business logic behind infrastructure.

runs.text: The bounded context size question is one of the most contentious in DDD practice — and there is no formula. Two failure modes bracket the useful range:
The
too-big bounded context

— often a monolith that grew without boundaries. Symptoms: the ubiquitous language contains ambiguous terms that mean different things to different teams; a change to 'customer' breaks unrelated features; the team cannot describe the model without qualification ('customer in the billing sense'). Evans describes this as 'model fragmentation' — the model serves too many masters to serve any of them well.
The
too-small bounded context

— a microservices over-decomposition. Symptoms: every user story requires changes across 5+ contexts; integration tests dominate the test suite; business logic is scattered across context boundaries with no single context owning a coherent capability. The interaction overhead consumes the integration savings.
Heuristics for right-sizing:

items.text: One team, one context.
If a context needs more than one team to build, it is either too large or needs internal sub-structure (modules within a context).
One ubiquitous language.
If the language has ambiguous terms that mean different things to different people inside the context, the context is too large.
Cohesive capability.
A context should own a recognisable business capability end-to-end. If you cannot name what business function the context performs, it is probably too small or too arbitrary.

runs.text: The microservices wave of the 2010s created many systems with too-small bounded contexts — 'nano-services' with one aggregate per service. The chatty integration overhead and distributed transaction complexity negated the isolation benefits. Sam Newman's 'Monolith to Microservices' (2019) documents the recovery patterns.

A bounded context that is too big has a model under strain — ambiguous language, too many competing concerns. One that is too small forces every feature change across too many context boundaries. The sweet spot is: one team, one clear language, one recognisable business capability.

cards.title: Strategic Design as a Continuous Discipline
cards.teaser: Strategic design is not a one-time architecture session — the business changes, teams restructure, new subdomains emerge as core, and old core subdomains become generic. The context map must be re-evaluated on a cadence that matches the rate of business change.

runs.text: A common misapplication of strategic DDD: run a big architecture workshop, draw the initial context map, ship the system, and never revisit the map. Six months later the system no longer reflects the business — a new partnership moved a supporting subdomain to core, an acquisition doubled the number of contexts, and a business pivot made the old model wrong.
Strategic design is a continuous practice for several reasons:

items.text: Core subdomains shift.
What was core in 2019 may be generic in 2024 — the market has caught up. A previously differentiating capability becomes a commodity. The investment posture must change.
Teams restructure.
Via Conway's Law, team reorganisations are context map reorganisations. If the map is not updated, it becomes misleading.
Integration patterns evolve.
An ACL that was the right choice for a transitional period may become unnecessary once a legacy system is decommissioned. Leaving dead integration scaffolding in place is technical debt.
New subdomains emerge.
Business strategy creates new capabilities. Without a strategic design review, new capabilities get bolted onto existing contexts rather than allocated to a new, clean boundary.

runs.text: A practical cadence: review the context map quarterly alongside business planning cycles. Large system changes — new partnerships, acquisitions, major product pivots — trigger an ad hoc strategic design session. Treat the context map as a living document under the same version control as the code.

Evans revised his thinking on strategic design in the DDD Reference (2015) and subsequent interviews: the initial strategic design conversation is a starting point, not a deliverable. The most valuable insight is that strategic design is an ongoing dialogue between technical and business leadership — not a one-time event that produces a diagram.

Strategic design is not a one-time workshop output. The business changes, the team structure changes, and what is core today can become generic tomorrow. Re-examine the context map on a regular cadence — not just at the start of a project.
